identity.title: Bad Seeing or Bad Thinking? Rewarding Perception for Multimodal Reasoning

problem.claim: Improve robust perception–reasoning synergy in vision-language models by identifying whether failures arise from perception or logic.

gap.claim: Existing architectural and agentic approaches can rely on static reasoning or impose substantial compute and engineering costs, while producing a perception–reasoning seesaw effect; the authors attribute this to ambiguous modality credit assignment.

contributions.claim: A reinforcement-learning framework that decomposes generation into interleaved perception and reasoning steps, enabling targeted supervision of perception.
Perception Verification uses a blindfolded-reasoning proxy to reward perceptual fidelity independently of reasoning outcomes.
Structured Verbal Verification and the Modality-Aware Credit Assignment mechanism use structured execution and error-source routing to scale verification and distinguish bad seeing from bad thinking.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors state that their framework resolves modality-credit ambiguity by independently verifying perception and routing rewards to the relevant modality-specific error.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that integrating these techniques enables a single VLM to achieve simultaneous performance gains across a wide task spectrum.

narrative_sequence.summary: Robust perception–reasoning synergy is presented as a central VLM goal, pursued through architectural designs and agentic workflows.
The abstract reports static reasoning, high compute and engineering burden, and a seesaw effect despite substantial investment.
The authors frame the bottleneck as ambiguous modality credit assignment: distinguishing bad seeing from bad thinking.
They introduce interleaved-step decomposition, Perception Verification, Structured Verbal Verification, and MoCA to supervise perception and route rewards by error source.

source_observation.claim: The abstract separates perception verification from reasoning outcomes and then routes rewards to the specific source of error.

lessons.interpretation: Separating error diagnosis from end-task success can make multimodal training signals more targeted.
lessons.application: For a multimodal method, define an intermediate modality-specific verification signal and an explicit mechanism assigning credit to perception versus reasoning.
lessons.exception: This move may be unsuitable when modality-specific correctness cannot be operationalized independently or when intermediate verification is unreliable.

unknowns: No task list, baseline results, metrics, sample sizes, or training conditions are provided for the reported simultaneous gains.
The abstract does not specify how blindfolded reasoning or structured verbal verification is implemented, nor how MoCA resolves ambiguous cases.
The claimed scope of the “wide task spectrum” is unspecified.
